name: Bianca Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I came to paid music late, after years at a shop counter. I play keyboard for a small theatre, record simple backing parts and teach two beginners, and I still ask the older player to listen when a chord feels wrong. I like the moment a singer trusts the first note; I dislike hauling the keyboard home after a short call.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What are the finances behind that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner fixes lifts, our grown children have their own homes, and we rent. We have about four months of bills saved and my music pay is ordinary, with a few other venues nearby. I use AI every day to draft set lists and move a tune into a singer’s key, then I check every note myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that a faster set list is welcome if someone still checks the notes. I already use AI for a first draft and do the final keyboard check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre calls and two pupils have held steady, and my partner’s lift work has kept coming. Four months saved leaves us room for a short gap, although rent still wants paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the theatre calls, recordings and two pupils, and ask for the next run’s paid rehearsal hours in writing. In the first plateau year I would save one quarter of each cleared extra backing-track fee after rent, food and travel toward six months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our current work. I do not need a new gadget to make a paid rehearsal count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the note check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A key change can put the singer outside their range. The tool gives me a starting point. My ears decide whether the AI key change fits the singer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a lighter keyboard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if cleared paid calls cover the price after rent and the reserve stays intact. Mine is heavy, but it works.

do: Keep **theatre, recordings and pupils** with written paid rehearsal hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the theatre can make a set list in seconds, but it should still pay the player who checks it. I would show the band only a cleaned recording I am allowed to use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The backing-track orders could thin out, and a theatre might cut paid preparation. The two pupils are small but real income; I would feel the loss at rent time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I would learn AI audio cleaning on my own licensed keyboard takes, compare the result to the original by ear and keep pupil recordings off public tools without permission. If two monthly backing orders disappear, I would look for a posted paid venue-front-desk role only if my secondary schooling qualifies and a written net wage after travel replaces the lost fees; I would keep theatre and pupils until a signed offer, and follow the same rule during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real piece of my pay shrinking. I can learn a tool and look for other work. Neither a tool nor a job search is a wage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a pupil recording to learn the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use only my own licensed takes at first. A family would have to agree in writing before any private lesson recording went into a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid trial at the desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would ask for the posted hours and pay first. I would not give up a paid rehearsal for an unpaid promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that 2028 thinking AGI could make booking sheets and recordings before robot keyboard players arrive around 2031. I would ask for the next run’s paid hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the backing-track calls to go and perhaps fewer paid theatre rehearsals in 2028. Four months saved is helpful, but losing both would bring rent into the conversation quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would confirm written theatre dates and keep the two pupils. In the first year after AGI arrives, if backing orders stop and rehearsals shrink, I would apply for an advertised paid venue-front-desk vacancy only if it accepts my secondary education and written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees; I would keep music income until the offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing two fee lines fast, though the four months saved and some local venues give me a little room. A venue-front-desk advert still has to turn into a paid offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your old shop work help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mention the years behind a counter, but I would read the vacancy requirements first. Experience is useful only if the employer accepts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would a robot matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A capable robot player is around 2031 in this card. The thinking work of booking and making a track changes in 2028, before that stage question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time to see whether the theatre keeps paying for real players. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot players follow around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Backing tracks may lose buyers, but I could use the years to learn a real desk system rather than wait for the last theatre cheque. I need venue-desk training that does not cost a paid rehearsal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep theatre, recordings and pupils, and ask the venue whether it offers paid-time training on its booking system for a posted front-desk opening. I would take that training only if it is funded, my secondary schooling is accepted and my paid music hours remain; in the first year after 2031, if backing orders and rehearsals fall, I would move only for a signed paid offer whose written net wage after travel replaces the loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording money over the next few years. Five years lets me check a real opening and learn the system without betting the rent on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a private course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the venue system changes and I cannot guess what another employer needs. I would take a funded course on paid time only for a real posted opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop teaching your two pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a signed offer gives enough net pay and hours to replace those fees too. Until then their Thursday lessons stay in the diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot keyboard players around 2039 are separate dates. I would ask the theatre for written rehearsal pay now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may choose fewer evening calls, but I have not set a retirement date. Our four months saved and my partner’s work support the next few years, not any promise about a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep the theatre and two pupils and save a quarter of cleared extra recording fees after rent, food and travel toward six months. Over the decade I would take only funded venue-system training on paid time for an actual posted desk role accepting my secondary education, without losing music hours; in the first year after 2036, if backing and rehearsal fees fall, I would move only on a signed written net offer after travel replacing those fees, keeping current work until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far end of recording pay. For now the theatre calls, pupils and partner’s work still cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a studio setup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A decade on a calendar is not a purchase order. I would keep my working keyboard and the four-month reserve intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no desk vacancy appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid music calls while they exist and ask other nearby venues about posted roles. I would not give up two pupils for a hypothetical title.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because both recordings and rehearsals could lose pay before I have a desk offer. Written theatre dates, a real vacancy, and funded training on paid time would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the singer whether the new key actually fits before you print the parts. A beautiful-looking score can still put a human voice in the wrong place.

headlineQuote: A beautiful-looking score can still put a human voice in the wrong place.
portrait: Bianca is a **junior keyboard player** who entered music after shop work and has secondary schooling.
She has **four months saved**, a lift-repairing partner, grown children, rent and ordinary music pay.
Her daily **AI set lists** get manual checks; she newly studies licensed audio cleaning with consent.
She considers a **venue desk** only with accepted schooling and a signed replacement wage, seeking funded training on longer timelines.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut recordings and rehearsals before she receives a desk offer.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written theatre dates**, an actual paid vacancy and funded training on paid time.
